signals.label: AI consensus, now two-way
signals.detail: Semis rebounded on Micron; Tepper trimmed, Burry short
signals.takeaway: Still the most-held/most-bought name across Q1 13Fs, and the AI trade healed fast: the June 23 Asian-led chip rout was bought back within two sessions as Micron's blowout earnings drove a June 25 semis rebound. But the top is two-sided — David Tepper trimmed NVDA and AMD in June, Michael Burry has loudly intensified his NVDA short (flagging customer-concentration and a disputed xAI GPU sale), and Sen. Whitehouse logged a six-figure NVDA sale. Consensus long, but the smart-money tape is split.

signals.name: MP Materials / rare earths
signals.label: Critical-minerals flashpoint
signals.detail: China blacklisted MP & USA Rare Earth (June 22)
signals.takeaway: On June 22 China's MOFCOM added MP Materials, USA Rare Earth and ~8 other US firms to its export-control list, retaliating for expanded US restrictions and re-igniting the ex-China rare-earth trade. China controls ~70% of mining and ~90% of processing/magnets, so each escalation raises the strategic value of Western names (MP — DoD a stakeholder — Lynas, Neo, Energy Fuels). A policy-driven, multi-name theme to watch alongside the June 30 Section 232 copper decision.

signals.label: Micron blowout — AI memory
signals.detail: Fiscal-Q3 beat drove a June 25 semis rebound
signals.takeaway: Micron's blowout fiscal-Q3 (AI/HBM memory demand and pricing) was the catalyst that reversed the June 23 chip rout, sending the stock +12% and SanDisk +14.7% on June 25 and dragging the whole semi complex higher. Institutional accumulation aligned with top retail mention rank — both leaning into the AI-memory upcycle; a core pick in the funds-favor-semis-over-software rotation.

signals.label: Mag-7 consensus
signals.detail: ~57% consensus; Ackman in, Gates Trust out
signals.takeaway: A top consensus holding with a vivid split: Pershing opened a ~15% position the same quarter the Gates Foundation Trust sold its last shares.

signals.name: SPDR Gold Shares
signals.label: Safe-haven unwind
signals.detail: Gold ~$4,040, sliding on a hawkish Fed
signals.takeaway: Firm real yields (10y ~4.4%, firm dollar) and a fully-unwound Iran war premium pulled gold to ~$4,040, deeper off its ~$4,724 peak though still +30%+ y/y on central-bank demand. A hike-biased June FOMC plus a hot 3.4% core-PCE print (lifting September hike odds toward ~50-68%) is a headwind for the non-yielding stagflation hedge; the July 14 June CPI and any eventual pivot are the next swings.

signals.name: Inflation / Fed
signals.label: Hawkish Fed, hot core PCE
signals.takeaway: The June 17 FOMC (Chair Warsh's first) held at 3.50-3.75% but leaned hawkish — nine of eighteen members project a 2026 hike, Warsh submitted no dot of his own, and the committee withheld forward guidance. A June 25/26 core-PCE at 3.4% y/y (headline 4.1%, hottest since 2023) plus a BofA 'series of hikes' call pushed market-implied September hike odds toward ~50-68%. The June CPI lands July 14; breakevens are squeezed between sticky core and a collapsing oil tail (WTI <$70).

signals.label: Buyback signal
signals.detail: Tencent buyback streak ran daily through June 25
signals.takeaway: One of HK's largest repurchase programs — Tencent kept buying back ~1.08-1.2M shares (~HK$500-501M) almost every trading day through June 25, ~26M shares cumulatively as the stock eased from ~HK$460 to ~HK$413. A near-mechanical, corporate-level conviction signal alongside its AI/gaming/fintech franchises; Xiaomi (new HK$20bn program), Li Auto and Kuaishou are running parallel HK buybacks.

signals.name: Energy Select Sector
signals.label: Congress vs. crude
signals.detail: Members keep buying energy as WTI falls below $70
signals.takeaway: Republican members (Hern's Coterra+Devon, Foxx's ARLP coal MLP) keep accumulating traditional energy on the power-demand thesis even as crude keeps sliding — WTI fell below $70 and Brent below $74 (lowest since February, ~40% off the wartime peak) after the US-Iran framework reopened Hormuz, lifted the naval blockade and granted Iran a 60-day oil-sales license. A tug-of-war between structural demand and a fully-deflated geopolitical premium.

congress.rationale: Disclosed June 23, the former Speaker (via her husband) bought 200 Intel call options (~$50 strike, March 2027 expiry) — her first trades since January 2026 and a large, leveraged bullish bet on the US semiconductor champion.
congress.deepDive: Pelosi's options trades are among the most closely watched in markets, and a seven-figure notional Intel call position is a conspicuous, high-conviction wager on a turnaround at the embattled chipmaker as US re-shoring, CHIPS-Act fab subsidies and AI demand converge. Buying deep-dated calls (March 2027) maximizes leverage and time for the thesis to play out, consistent with her pattern of long-dated, in-or-near-the-money call buying on mega-cap tech. The timing — late May, disclosed late June — lands amid an intense AI/semis tape that saw a June 23 chip rout reverse on Micron's blowout. As a senior member with deep visibility into tech and trade policy, even routine Pelosi disclosures draw STOCK Act scrutiny and retail copy-trading.

congress.rationale: A companion bet to the Intel calls: 200 Uber call options (~$50 strike, March 2027 expiry), a leveraged bullish position on the rideshare/delivery and autonomy platform.
congress.deepDive: Pairing Uber with Intel in the same late-May filing extends Pelosi's preference for long-dated calls on large, liquid franchises with secular tailwinds — here the AV/robotaxi optionality, delivery scale and improving free-cash-flow profile that have made Uber a hedge-fund favorite. The March 2027 expiry again gives the thesis ample runway. Uber is also a top conviction holding among super-investors (Ackman's Pershing Square), so the trade aligns institutional and political-insider positioning. The size and leverage make it a clear directional call rather than diversification, and it draws the usual STOCK Act and copy-trade attention.

congress.rationale: The Florida Democrat added Gilead Sciences, a defensive large-cap biotech, within a broader portfolio that leans toward AI and defense (AVGO, NVDA, ADI).
congress.deepDive: Moskowitz is an active trader whose disclosures span healthcare, semiconductors and defense, and the Gilead buy adds a steady, dividend-paying biotech to a book otherwise tilted toward AI-infrastructure beneficiaries. Gilead's HIV franchise and pipeline make it a lower-beta holding that can cushion a growth-heavy portfolio if a rate-driven multiple compression hits high-flyers. Pairing the GILD purchase with a sale of drug-distributor Cencora (COR) the same day reads as a rotation within healthcare rather than a sector call. As a member subject to STOCK Act reporting, his frequent two-sided trading draws routine scrutiny.

congress.rationale: The Nevada Democrat continued liquidating a concentrated Full House Resorts stake, part of an ongoing effort to convert individual shares received in her divorce into diversified ETFs and index funds.
congress.deepDive: Lee has disclosed a long series of FLL disposals since 2025 as she transfers holdings received in her divorce into ETFs, index funds and mutual funds, and Full House's CEO has previously described some sales as planned transactions. Because Full House Resorts is a casino operator tied to her Las Vegas-area district, the repeated and sizable sells draw STOCK Act scrutiny, though her office frames them as diversification rather than market timing. The latest sale falls in the $250K-$500K band, among the larger single congressional disclosures in early June. The pattern reads as continued de-risking of a legacy concentrated position rather than a new directional view.

congress.rationale: The North Carolina Republican bought Alliance Resource Partners, a coal producer and high-yield MLP, aligning with a pro-fossil-fuel, income tilt.
congress.deepDive: Alliance Resource Partners is one of the largest US coal producers and pays a high distribution yield, making it a popular income play among energy-friendly Republican members. Foxx, a senior House member and former Education and Workforce Committee chair, has a history of energy and dividend-oriented holdings. The coal bet fits a 2026 theme of traditional-energy accumulation tied to rising electricity demand from data centers and electrification. As an MLP, ARLP also carries distinctive pass-through tax characteristics relevant to disclosure.

congress.rationale: The Oklahoma Republican added Coterra Energy, an oil-and-gas producer squarely aligned with his home-state energy economy.
congress.deepDive: Hern, a wealthy McDonald's franchisee turned congressman, frequently trades energy names that mirror Oklahoma's hydrocarbon-heavy economy. The Coterra purchase came alongside a Devon Energy buy, doubling down on domestic exploration and production. As a senior member of the House Ways and Means Committee and former Republican Policy Committee chair, his energy positions intersect with tax and energy-policy levers he helps write. The paired E&P buys read as a clear bullish bet on US oil and gas through 2026.

congress.rationale: A second energy purchase (Devon Energy) reinforcing Hern's concentrated bet on domestic oil and gas producers.
congress.deepDive: Buying Devon alongside Coterra in the same filing shows Hern leaning hard into upstream energy rather than diversifying broadly. Devon's shareholder-return model and Permian exposure make it a popular income-and-value energy pick consistent with his prior trading patterns. His Ways and Means perch over tax policy gives energy-sector trades a policy-adjacent flavor worth flagging. The move tracks a wider 2026 pattern of Republican members accumulating traditional energy as power demand rises.

congress.rationale: The Michigan Republican bought Boeing as part of a broad multi-sector basket spanning defense, industrials, consumer and tech.
congress.deepDive: Walberg's filing was unusually wide-ranging, adding Boeing, Apple, Amazon, Caterpillar, L3Harris, Under Armour and a specialty lending fund in one disclosure. The mix suggests diversified accumulation rather than a targeted thesis, with an aerospace/defense lean reinforced by pairing Boeing with L3Harris. As a senior member of the House Energy and Commerce Committee, his tech and telecom-adjacent holdings draw oversight interest. The Boeing position is a cyclical industrial bet within a clear buy-the-market posture.

congress.rationale: A defense-contractor purchase (L3Harris) sized larger than most lines in Walberg's basket, signaling conviction in elevated defense spending.
congress.deepDive: The L3Harris buy, in the $15K-$50K bracket, is among the larger lines in Walberg's basket and points to conviction in defense and aerospace primes amid sustained Pentagon budgets and global tensions. Pairing LHX with Boeing reinforces an aerospace/defense tilt. Walberg's Energy and Commerce seat does not directly oversee defense procurement, slightly reducing the conflict angle, but the holding still ties him to a policy-sensitive sector. The size relative to his other buys marks it as a higher-conviction position.

congress.rationale: The prolific New Jersey Democrat added Analog Devices, tilting toward semiconductors alongside other chip and security names.
congress.deepDive: Gottheimer is one of the most active traders in the House, with hundreds of millions in lifetime disclosed volume routed through managed accounts. The Analog Devices buy came alongside purchases of Palo Alto Networks, SanDisk, Fabrinet and Microsoft options plus sales of Nestle and Berkshire, signaling a tilt toward semiconductors and security infrastructure amid the AI buildout. As a senior member of the House Financial Services Committee, his trading draws STOCK Act scrutiny. Because the trades run through managed accounts, the direct signaling value is muted, but the aggregate direction is a clear growth/semis tilt.

congress.rationale: A SanDisk purchase, a bet on NAND/storage memory demand amid AI-driven data growth, part of the same semiconductor-heavy basket.
congress.deepDive: SanDisk, the storage business spun out of Western Digital, is a leveraged play on NAND flash pricing and AI-related data-storage demand. Adding it alongside Analog Devices, Palo Alto Networks and Fabrinet deepens Gottheimer's semiconductor and security exposure. The purchase fits his pattern of active, momentum-aware trading through Morgan Stanley managed accounts. As a Financial Services Committee member, his tech trades remain under STOCK Act scrutiny even though they are managed externally.

congress.rationale: The prolific New Jersey Democrat bought Lumentum Holdings, an optical-components maker leveraged to AI-datacenter networking demand, while selling defensive names Abbott and Intuit.
congress.deepDive: Lumentum supplies lasers and optical transceivers central to the high-speed interconnects inside AI data centers, so the buy extends Gottheimer's running tilt toward the AI-infrastructure supply chain (he recently added Analog Devices, SanDisk and Fabrinet). Pairing the LITE purchase with sales of Abbott Laboratories and Intuit rotates from defensive healthcare and software toward optical-networking hardware, echoing the broader institutional move to favor AI 'picks-and-shovels' over platforms. As a senior House Financial Services Committee member his trades draw STOCK Act scrutiny, though they run through Morgan Stanley managed accounts, muting the direct signal. The direction nonetheless reinforces a clear AI-hardware bias.

congress.rationale: A sizable sale of NVIDIA, the AI poster child, locking in gains from a richly valued position — notable from a senator who publicly criticizes congressional stock trading.
congress.deepDive: Whitehouse has long advocated ethics reform and supports restricting member trading, making his own six-figure NVIDIA sale politically conspicuous. The trade, paired with an Oracle sale, points to de-risking from high-multiple AI infrastructure names after a strong run. As a senior member of the Senate Judiciary Committee, his transactions feed the broader debate over whether lawmakers should hold individual equities at all. The $100K-$250K size is large relative to typical House disclosures and amplifies the optics.

congress.rationale: Exiting Oracle alongside NVIDIA, reinforcing a defensive rotation out of AI/cloud infrastructure equities.
congress.deepDive: Oracle has been re-rated higher on the strength of its cloud and AI data-center contracts, so Whitehouse's sale likely reflects profit-taking near elevated valuations. Combined with the much larger NVIDIA exit, the filing reads as a deliberate reduction of concentrated tech exposure rather than a one-off. For a senator who champions financial-disclosure transparency, methodically documenting these sales is consistent with his public posture even as critics question the holdings themselves. The move mirrors a wider 2026 theme of insiders trimming AI winners.

congress.rationale: The Florida Republican sold Rexford Industrial, an industrial REIT, trimming real-estate exposure.
congress.deepDive: Rexford Industrial is a Southern California-focused industrial REIT whose shares have been pressured by softening warehouse demand and rate sensitivity. Webster's sale of REXR removes a niche real-estate holding and may reflect caution on industrial property fundamentals or simple rebalancing. As a long-serving House member, his relatively infrequent trades draw modest scrutiny. The disposal fits a 2026 pattern of members trimming rate-sensitive REIT exposure.

superInvestors.name: Berkshire Hathaway
superInvestors.rationale: Berkshire initiated a brand-new ~39.8M share stake in Delta Air Lines worth roughly $2.65B, making it the firm's largest new holding of the quarter.
superInvestors.deepDive: This is a notable re-entry into the airline sector, which Buffett famously dumped entirely in 2020 calling it a mistake. The buy looks like a cyclical, deep-value bet on a distressed airline price amid fuel-cost and demand concerns. It is among the first major equity initiations under Greg Abel's expanded role, suggesting a willingness to revisit names Buffett had sworn off. At ~$2.6B it is a meaningful but not portfolio-defining position within a ~$263B book.

superInvestors.name: Berkshire Hathaway
superInvestors.rationale: Berkshire boosted its Alphabet Class A stake by roughly 204% to about 54.2M shares (~$15.6B) and opened a new Class C (GOOG) position.
superInvestors.deepDive: The aggressive add turns Alphabet into one of Berkshire's largest tech bets, an unusual lean into a mega-cap growth name for a value-oriented firm. The stated thesis centers on Alphabet's AI leadership through Gemini and Google Cloud plus its dominant search and advertising cash flows. Doubling down while simultaneously trimming financials like Visa and Mastercard signals a rotation toward AI-infrastructure beneficiaries. The new Class C tranche suggests opportunistic share-class arbitrage on top of the core conviction.

superInvestors.name: Berkshire Hathaway
superInvestors.rationale: Berkshire fully exited Visa, divesting roughly $2.91B, part of a broad sell-down of positions including Mastercard, UnitedHealth and Amazon.
superInvestors.deepDive: Dumping both Visa and Mastercard (~$5B combined) marks a sharp reversal on the payment-network duopoly Berkshire had held for years. The exits coincided with the firm remaining a net seller and trimming its holding count materially. With a ~$397B cash pile, the moves reinforce a defensive, capital-preservation posture in the Abel transition. The rotation out of payments and into Alphabet/Delta reflects a meaningful reshuffling of sector exposure.

superInvestors.name: Berkshire Hathaway
superInvestors.rationale: Berkshire completely exited UnitedHealth Group, selling roughly $1.66B worth of the managed-care insurer.
superInvestors.deepDive: The UNH exit removes Berkshire from a healthcare name that had been under regulatory and operational pressure. Combined with exits from Domino's, Aon, Pool Corp and Amazon, it shows a clean-up of smaller, lower-conviction positions. Selling into a beaten-down healthcare sector suggests the investment team saw better risk-reward elsewhere rather than averaging down. It fits the quarter's overall theme of concentrating the book into fewer, higher-conviction holdings.

superInvestors.name: Soros Fund Management
superInvestors.rationale: Soros Fund Management increased its NVIDIA stake during Q1 2026, alongside adds in Taiwan Semiconductor and Electronic Arts.
superInvestors.deepDive: The NVIDIA add signals continued conviction in the AI-compute leader even at elevated valuations, consistent with Soros's opportunistic, momentum-aware style. It came as the fund grew its overall 13F book to roughly $9.1B across 263 positions. Pairing the NVDA add with TSM exposure reflects a full-stack semiconductor bet on AI infrastructure. The simultaneous trimming of AMZN, GOOGL, MSFT and CRM suggests rotation within mega-cap tech rather than a broad risk-off.

superInvestors.name: Soros Fund Management
superInvestors.rationale: Soros initiated a new position in TSM put options, a hedged stance on the chip foundry even as it added to common TSM exposure.
superInvestors.deepDive: Buying TSM puts is a classic Soros macro-hedge overlay, expressing caution on semiconductor cyclicality or geopolitical Taiwan risk while still holding the equity. The combined long-stock-plus-puts positioning reflects a desire for asymmetric protection rather than an outright directional call. It is emblematic of the fund's special-situations and tactical-hedging DNA under its current managers. Investors should read this as risk management, not a wholesale bearish bet on chips.

superInvestors.name: Soros Fund Management
superInvestors.rationale: Soros opened a new stake in Berkshire Hathaway Class B shares during Q1 2026.
superInvestors.deepDive: Adding Berkshire is a notable defensive, quality tilt for a fund better known for aggressive macro trades. It may reflect a desire for a diversified, cash-rich equity proxy during a period of elevated market uncertainty. The position sits alongside other new buys, pointing to a broadening rather than concentration of the book. Buying Berkshire just as Berkshire itself sat on ~$397B cash is an implicit endorsement of capital-preservation positioning.

superInvestors.name: Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation Trust
superInvestors.rationale: The Gates Foundation Trust sold its final ~7.7M Microsoft shares (~$3.2B), holding zero Microsoft for the first time since its founding.
superInvestors.deepDive: This is a landmark, symbolic move ending the Trust's decades-long relationship with the company Bill Gates co-founded. It completes a multi-year wind-down driven by diversification and liquidity needs to fund the foundation's accelerated giving timeline. With Microsoft gone, Berkshire Hathaway (~25.8%) and Waste Management (~20%) now anchor the ~$31.7B portfolio. The exit removes single-stock concentration risk but also caps the Trust's exposure to the AI-driven upside Microsoft has captured.

superInvestors.name: Duquesne Family Office
superInvestors.rationale: Druckenmiller's Duquesne fully exited its entire 385,000-share Alphabet Class A position in Q1 2026.
superInvestors.deepDive: The complete Alphabet exit is striking given Berkshire was aggressively adding the same name in the same quarter, highlighting divergent views among elite investors. Druckenmiller is known for rapid conviction shifts, and dumping a mega-cap AI winner may reflect profit-taking or a macro-driven de-risking. It came alongside a dramatic Amazon cut, suggesting a deliberate reduction of mega-cap tech beta. The move fits Duquesne's high-turnover profile, with many full exits and new positions in the quarter.

superInvestors.name: Duquesne Family Office
superInvestors.rationale: Duquesne slashed its Amazon stake from 737,940 shares to just 9,539 shares, a near-total liquidation.
superInvestors.deepDive: Cutting Amazon by ~99% effectively closes a former core position, reinforcing Druckenmiller's pullback from mega-cap tech. The token remaining stake may be a placeholder to keep the name on the radar for re-entry. Paired with the Alphabet exit, it signals concern about valuations or macro headwinds for the largest tech names. Druckenmiller has historically rotated aggressively between growth and defensives, and this looks like a decisive risk reduction.

superInvestors.name: Duquesne Family Office
superInvestors.rationale: Duquesne opened a new ~195,955-share Broadcom position (~$60.65M), rotating semiconductor exposure toward the AI-networking leader.
superInvestors.deepDive: Buying Broadcom while exiting Alphabet and Amazon shows Druckenmiller concentrating his AI bet on the picks-and-shovels infrastructure layer rather than the platform giants. Broadcom's custom-silicon and networking franchise is a direct beneficiary of hyperscaler AI capex. The move aligns with a broader market theme of investors favoring semis over software/platforms in Q1 2026. New stakes in Caris Life Sciences and Revolution Medicines round out a tilt toward AI-enabled diagnostics and biotech.

superInvestors.name: Duquesne Family Office
superInvestors.rationale: Natera became Duquesne's single largest holding at roughly 18% of the ~$3.4B portfolio in Q1 2026.
superInvestors.deepDive: Making a genetic-testing/diagnostics company the top position is a high-conviction, concentrated bet unusual even for Druckenmiller. It reflects a thesis on precision medicine and molecular diagnostics as a structural growth area. Combined with new biotech buys in Caris and Revolution Medicines, it shows a clear healthcare-innovation theme building in the book. The concentration underscores Druckenmiller's willingness to size up his best ideas.

superInvestors.name: Pershing Square
superInvestors.rationale: Ackman's Pershing Square initiated a large new Microsoft position equal to roughly 15% of its ~$13.7B portfolio.
superInvestors.deepDive: The Microsoft buy is a significant new mega-cap tech addition for a famously concentrated ~10-stock portfolio. It signals Ackman's conviction in Microsoft's AI monetization through Copilot and Azure as a durable, high-quality compounder. The position instantly became a top holding alongside Brookfield, Amazon and Uber. Notably, Ackman added Microsoft just as the Gates Foundation was selling its last shares, a vivid illustration of opposing institutional views.

superInvestors.name: Pershing Square
superInvestors.rationale: Pershing Square increased its Amazon stake, lifting it to roughly 17% of the portfolio and one of the top two holdings.
superInvestors.deepDive: The Amazon add deepens Ackman's bet on a mega-cap whose retail margins and AWS cloud/AI growth he views as undervalued. It contrasts sharply with Druckenmiller, who nearly eliminated Amazon in the same quarter. Concentrating further into Amazon and Microsoft reflects Ackman's strategy of owning a handful of dominant, cash-generative franchises. The move keeps Pershing Square's tech weighting high even as it trimmed Brookfield and Uber.

superInvestors.name: Pershing Square
superInvestors.rationale: Pershing Square fully exited its Hilton Worldwide position in Q1 2026.
superInvestors.deepDive: Selling Hilton ends a long-held, successful hospitality investment that Ackman had praised for years as a high-quality asset-light compounder. The exit likely helped fund the new Microsoft stake, reflecting a reallocation toward AI-exposed mega-cap tech. It may also signal caution on consumer/travel cyclicals at this point in the cycle. For a portfolio this concentrated, removing a name entirely is a meaningful conviction shift rather than routine trimming.

superInvestors.name: Bridgewater Associates
superInvestors.rationale: Bridgewater boosted its NVIDIA exposure as part of a broad rotation into semiconductor and AI-infrastructure stocks.
superInvestors.deepDive: The NVDA add anchors a clear strategic tilt toward AI hardware, with simultaneous increases in Broadcom and Micron. For a systematic, macro-driven shop, leaning into chips reflects models favoring the AI-capex theme. The rotation was funded partly by exiting enterprise-software names like Salesforce, ServiceNow, Workday and Adobe. It signals Bridgewater's view that hardware beneficiaries offer better risk-reward than software at current valuations.

superInvestors.name: Bridgewater Associates
superInvestors.rationale: Bridgewater opened a new Taiwan Semiconductor position alongside new stakes in Alphabet and Nucor.
superInvestors.deepDive: Initiating TSM completes Bridgewater's full-stack semiconductor bet spanning foundry (TSM), GPUs (NVDA), networking (AVGO) and memory (MU). The pairing with a new Alphabet stake adds platform-level AI exposure on top of the hardware layer. The new Nucor position hints at a parallel reflation/industrial-cyclical theme in the firm's models. Within a ~$22B equity book still topped by broad index ETFs, these single-name adds represent deliberate active tilts.

superInvestors.name: Bridgewater Associates
superInvestors.rationale: Bridgewater exited Salesforce, part of a broad pullback from enterprise-software names including ServiceNow, Workday and Adobe.
superInvestors.deepDive: Dumping software while loading chips is the cleanest expression of Bridgewater's Q1 2026 rotation thesis. The view appears to be that AI is compressing software margins and moats while boosting demand for the underlying compute. Exiting multiple SaaS leaders at once suggests a systematic, factor-driven decision rather than a single-name call. It positions the firm to benefit if AI-infrastructure spending continues to outrun software re-acceleration.

superInvestors.name: Scion Asset Management
superInvestors.rationale: Michael Burry initiated a new full-sized MercadoLibre position, buying after the stock dropped ~13% on Q1 earnings.
superInvestors.deepDive: Burry took the unusual step of disclosing the MELI buy directly on his Substack, signaling high conviction in the Latin American e-commerce and fintech leader at a beaten-down price. It is a classic Burry contrarian move: buying quality into a post-earnings panic. MELI sits in a concentrated nine-name portfolio, so it represents a meaningful slug of the book. The bet expresses confidence in MELI's durable growth despite near-term margin or FX concerns that spooked the market.

superInvestors.name: Scion Asset Management
superInvestors.rationale: Scion built a new full-sized Lululemon stake near a multi-year low.
superInvestors.deepDive: Buying Lululemon at multi-year lows is vintage Burry deep-value contrarianism on a former growth darling that fell out of favor. The thesis likely centers on a still-strong brand and balance sheet trading at a compressed valuation after a growth scare. It joins new buys in Adobe and PayPal, forming a basket of beaten-down large-cap consumer and tech names. The concentration into just nine positions amplifies the payoff if these turnarounds materialize.

superInvestors.name: Scion Asset Management
superInvestors.rationale: Burry fully liquidated his entire Chinese technology basket, exiting Alibaba, JD.com and Baidu in Q1 2026.
superInvestors.deepDive: The complete China exit reverses Burry's high-profile prior bullishness on cheap Chinese internet names. It mirrors David Tepper trimming China in the same period, suggesting shared caution on Chinese equities amid policy or geopolitical risk. Rotating the proceeds into MELI, LULU, ADBE and PYPL shifts the book toward Western beaten-down large caps. Notably, the long-only 13F shows no put options, though Burry's filings historically understate his options book.

superInvestors.name: Appaloosa
superInvestors.rationale: David Tepper boosted Whirlpool by nearly 2,000% quarter-over-quarter, building a ~$432.3M position (~5.85% of the portfolio).
superInvestors.deepDive: The massive Whirlpool add is Appaloosa's most aggressive single move of the quarter, a deep-cyclical, contrarian bet on a beaten-down appliance maker. The thesis likely hinges on a housing/consumer-durables recovery and Whirlpool's depressed valuation and high dividend. It exemplifies Tepper's willingness to size up out-of-favor cyclicals when he sees asymmetric upside. The buy sits within a ~$5.9B, ~31-position portfolio still led by Amazon, Micron and Alphabet.

superInvestors.name: Appaloosa
superInvestors.rationale: Tepper added substantially to Amazon (shares up ~98%), keeping it the top holding at ~15% of the portfolio.
superInvestors.deepDive: Nearly doubling the Amazon stake shows Tepper leaning into mega-cap tech even as he trims some winners elsewhere. The move diverges from Druckenmiller's near-exit of Amazon, again highlighting split views among top investors. Tepper's thesis likely rests on AWS AI growth and improving retail profitability. Combined with big adds to Uber and Vistra, it reflects a barbell of mega-cap tech plus cyclicals and power/AI-energy names.

superInvestors.name: Appaloosa
superInvestors.rationale: Appaloosa trimmed its Alibaba exposure, selling roughly $227.6M of the Chinese e-commerce giant.
superInvestors.deepDive: Cutting Alibaba marks a partial retreat from the China-tech thesis Tepper championed loudly in late 2024. It echoes Burry's full China exit in the same quarter, signaling broader hedge-fund caution on Chinese equities. Tepper appears to be reallocating toward US cyclicals (Whirlpool, Vistra) and mega-cap tech (Amazon, Uber). The trim is a reduction rather than a full exit, suggesting he still sees residual value but wants lower China beta.

superInvestors.name: Tiger Global
superInvestors.rationale: Tiger Global initiated a new MercadoLibre position in Q1 2026, one of seven new buys in the quarter.
superInvestors.deepDive: Tiger and Burry both bought MELI in the same quarter, a notable convergence of a growth-oriented crossover fund and a deep-value contrarian on the Latin American leader. For Tiger, MELI fits its long-standing focus on dominant internet and e-commerce platforms. The buy came amid an active quarter that included seven new buys and seven full exits. It complements Tiger's heavy AI/tech tilt led by Alphabet, NVIDIA, Amazon and TSM.

superInvestors.name: Tiger Global
superInvestors.rationale: Tiger Global increased its Taiwan Semiconductor stake by ~49%, lifting it to a top-4 holding at ~8% of the ~$22.8B portfolio.
superInvestors.deepDive: The TSM add deepens Tiger's AI-infrastructure exposure, complementing large positions in NVIDIA and Broadcom (also added). It reflects conviction that the AI-capex cycle still has room to run at the foundry level. The buy aligns with parallel moves by Bridgewater and Soros into TSM the same quarter, a clear cross-fund consensus on chips. Within a portfolio anchored by Alphabet and NVIDIA, the add reinforces a concentrated bet on the AI-compute supply chain.

superInvestors.name: Tiger Global
superInvestors.rationale: Tiger Global boosted Applied Materials by ~85%, one of its largest percentage adds of the quarter.
superInvestors.deepDive: Adding Applied Materials extends Tiger's semiconductor bet to the chip-equipment layer that supplies the entire foundry ecosystem. It signals confidence that AI-driven fab buildouts will sustain capital-equipment demand. Paired with the TSM and Broadcom adds, it shows Tiger constructing a full-stack semis exposure rather than relying solely on NVIDIA. The move continues the firm's recovery-era pivot back toward high-conviction public tech after its 2022 drawdown.

insiders.rationale: Tencent repurchased ~1.2 million shares for ~HK$500.7 million on 25 June 2026, the latest in a near-mechanical daily buyback streak (~1.08-1.2M shares / ~HK$500-501M almost every trading session through June) that has cumulatively retired ~26 million shares as the stock eased from ~HK$460 to ~HK$413.
insiders.deepDive: Company buybacks are a strong corporate-level conviction signal, and Tencent runs one of the largest repurchase programs in Hong Kong, returning capital while supporting the share price. The relentless daily repurchases through late May and all of June reflect a commitment to shrinking the share count and offsetting dilution from share-based compensation, with management leaning in harder as the price drifted lower. For holders of 0700, buybacks at this scale are accretive to per-share value and underscore the board's view that the stock is undervalued relative to its gaming, fintech and AI-cloud franchises. Tencent is not alone — Xiaomi (a new HK$20bn program plus a HK$4bn automatic buyback), Li Auto and Kuaishou are all running parallel HK repurchases. Unlike a director's open-market purchase, an issuer repurchase signals management's capital-allocation confidence rather than a single insider's personal bet, but the read-through is similarly bullish.

insiders.rationale: Newmont's CEO sold 3,882 shares (~$409K) on 1 June 2026 under a pre-arranged 10b5-1 plan, alongside a ~3,000-share (~$316K) sale by EVP Peter Toth — routine, plan-based selling at the world's largest gold miner (a top GDX holding) into elevated bullion prices.
insiders.deepDive: These are scheduled 10b5-1 disposals rather than discretionary, conviction-driven sells, so the signal is muted — executives routinely diversify into strength, and gold near record territory (~$4,000+) makes profit-taking unremarkable. As the largest US-filing gold producer and a core GDX constituent, Newmont insider activity is a useful read on miner sentiment, and the absence of any open-market buying alongside these sales is consistent with a sector that has already re-rated hard year-to-date. Note that most large GDX/SILJ miners are Canadian foreign private issuers that report on Canada's SEDI rather than US Form 4, so Newmont and Coeur are among the few that surface in SEC filings. The plan-based nature limits the bearish read, but persistent executive selling caps any narrative of insiders chasing the gold rally higher.

insiders.rationale: Coeur Mining's VP/Controller & CAO sold 39,000 shares (~$725K) on 1 June; separately EVP Exploration Aoife McGrath made a small open-market BUY of 635 shares (~$10.8K) on 12 June — a mixed but net-selling read at the silver/gold producer (a SILJ/GDX name).
insiders.deepDive: Coeur is one of the few US-domiciled precious-metals miners that files Form 4, making it a window into silver-complex insider sentiment that the largely-Canadian SILJ/SLVP universe otherwise hides on SEDI. The controller-level sale is administrative/diversification in character rather than a directional call, while the small EVP open-market purchase is a modest genuine-conviction buy — together a wash that leans slightly to distribution into the strong precious-metals tape. With silver whipsawing in the high-$50s to low-$60s and gold off its peak, the lack of sizable open-market buying suggests insiders see fair-to-full value after a powerful multi-quarter run rather than a fresh entry point. As always, plan-based and compensation-related transactions dominate miner Form 4 flow, so the signal is incremental, not decisive.

insiders.rationale: US asset manager Capital Group bought 19.3 million Singtel shares on the open market on 6 May 2026, lifting its total stake to ~838 million shares (~5.1%), crossing the 5% substantial-shareholder disclosure threshold.
insiders.deepDive: This makes Capital Group likely the second-largest Singtel holder after Temasek (~51.5%). The accumulation at an average of S$4.67 signals conviction from a long-only global manager as Singtel's capital-recycling strategy (the KKR/STT GDC data-centre deal and asset monetisation), a new S$2bn buyback and improved associate contributions drive a re-rating. A large active manager crossing 5% is meaningful: it reflects index-plus active demand for Singtel as a yield-plus-growth telco proxy, and adds a stable institutional anchor to the register. It is a buy by an outside substantial holder rather than a director, so it speaks to external valuation conviction rather than management signalling.

insiders.rationale: DBS CEO Tan Su Shan sold 100,000 DBS shares on the open market at S$60.12 each on 15 May 2026, leaving her with about 1.3 million shares (0.048% of the bank), shortly after the stock first pushed above S$60.
insiders.deepDive: The sale came days after DBS reported 1Q2026 net profit of S$2.93 billion (up 1% y-o-y and 24% q-o-q) and as the stock hit record territory near a S$173 billion market cap. As Singapore's largest lender's first female CEO (who succeeded Piyush Gupta in March 2025), Tan still retains a sizeable 1.3 million-share holding, so this is a partial profit-taking/liquidity trim rather than a loss of confidence. CEO sells into all-time highs are common and often tax or diversification-driven, but they can cap near-term sentiment given DBS's elevated valuation and the market's sensitivity to falling rates compressing net interest margins. The modest size relative to her remaining stake limits the negative signal. DBS continues to run a S$3bn buyback programme through 2027.
